name: WEIRD Samples Critique
description: The overwhelming majority of published behavioral-science research draws its participant samples from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies -- a narrow and, on many measured psychological dimensions, statistically unusual slice of humanity -- meaning many 'universal' findings in the literature may not generalize as broadly as their framing implies.
design_relevance_note: A standing caveat for any design team building for a genuinely global or culturally diverse user base: a cited behavioral-science finding's original sample composition is directly relevant to how confidently it should be assumed to hold for users outside that same narrow demographic slice.
prevalence_note: Foundational to how confidently any single behavioral-science finding should be generalized across cultures -- underlies this corpus's own dialectic-verification population-generalizability caveat, though the acronym itself is more an academic/meta-science term than everyday design-practice vocabulary.

findings.description: A review of the comparative database across the behavioral sciences finds that research routinely published in the field's top journals draws its samples almost exclusively from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies, and that WEIRD samples are frequent statistical outliers relative to the rest of the human species across many domains — visual perception, fairness and cooperation, spatial reasoning, categorization and inferential induction, moral reasoning, reasoning styles, self-concept and related motivations, and the heritability of IQ. The authors argue there is no a priori basis for assuming a finding demonstrated in a WEIRD sample generalizes to humans broadly, and call for structural changes in how the behavioral sciences sample and report findings.
findings.source_title: The weirdest people in the world?

findings.description: Across preregistered direct replications of 28 classic and contemporary psychology effects run in 125 samples spanning 36 countries (N = 15,305), replication effect sizes were systematically smaller than the originally published effect sizes (median Cohen's d fell from 0.60 in the originals to 0.15 in the replications), and only about half the effects reached conventional statistical significance in the same direction as the original. Despite this general replication shortfall, exploratory comparisons found little heterogeneity in effect sizes specifically between WEIRD and less-WEIRD cultural samples — cumulatively, variability in results was attributable far more to which effect was being studied than to the culture, sample, or setting it was studied in.
findings.effect_size: 54% of 28 replications significant, same direction as original (50% at strict p<.0001); median Cohen's d fell from 0.60 (original) to 0.15 (replication); little heterogeneity attributable to WEIRD vs. less-WEIRD sample split specifically
findings.source_title: Many Labs 2: Investigating Variation in Replicability Across Samples and Settings
findings.source_venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

applications.title: The Müller-Lyer illusion isn't universal: a 17-culture study found some groups barely see it at all
applications.description: Segall, Campbell & Herskovits' 1966 book 'The Influence of Culture on Visual Perception' (Bobbs-Merrill) tested susceptibility to the Müller-Lyer illusion -- the classic 'which line is longer' arrow-shaped illusion, then and now a staple example in perception research and design-adjacent writing about how the human visual system can be fooled -- across 17 groups spanning both Western and non-Western cultures. Susceptibility varied substantially by culture, with Kalahari hunter-gatherer groups among the least susceptible of all groups tested. The researchers' own explanation, since known as the 'carpentered world' hypothesis: Western populations' constant visual exposure to rectangular buildings, furniture, and right angles trains a depth-interpretation heuristic that the illusion exploits -- a heuristic that has little reason to develop, and correspondingly little effect, in environments without that same built-rectilinear-angle exposure. A perceptual effect treated as a fixed, universal fact about human vision turned out to be substantially shaped by which population was actually tested.
applications.industry_context: Cross-cultural psychology / perception research -- not a product-design deployment, but a real, checkable instance of exactly the generalization risk this BiasHeuristic warns design teams about.
applications.ethical_note: A research-methodology finding about the limits of generalizing from a narrow sample, with no persuasion or manipulation dimension to grade -- the same posture as this corpus's existing Publication Bias and Replication Crisis Applications, which are real documented instances of a meta-scientific phenomenon rather than product deployments.
